newsitem.title: TAIWAN: China details rules for Taiwan shipping links.
newsitem.headline: China details rules for Taiwan shipping links.

text.p: China's communications ministry on Tuesday announced detailed rules about direct shipping links with Taiwan and would start receiving applications from shipping firms, the Economic Daily News reported on Wednesday.

The rules were sent to related Chinese government agencies, requiring them to submit application documents to the communications ministry within nine days after the receipt of applications from interested shipping firms, the paper said.
The ministry would take another 45 days to review the applications.
The newspaper estimated a total of nine shipping firms would be approved to commence direct shipping between the two sides, around the end of 1996 or early 1997.

Among the nine, five Taiwan shipping firms are expected to receive approval. They are: Yang Ming Marine, Uniglory Marine, Wan Hai Lines, Nan Tai Enterprises, and Chinese Maritime Transport, the newspaper said.
China had announced on August 20 rules governing direct links across the Taiwan Strait, but gave no details.
A Taiwan communications ministry official told Reuters on Wednesday: "We are now trying to confirm the report. If it's true, it's surely a good news, a good beginning.

"We hope the cross-strait direct link can start as soon as possible. We have proposed the opening since last year, now we welcome communist China's ships to start to apply to us for the direct-link business."

On Tuesday, in an apparent easing of Taiwan's almost five-decade ban on direct mainland shipping, the island's communications ministry said Premier Lien Chan approved a scheme to allow foreign-flagged ships to sail directly between Taiwan and China.
The move, shipping executives say, might force domestic ships from the two sides to reflag their ships under third-country registration, so as not to be left out of the lucrative new business.
Beijing had baulked at earlier Taiwan proposals for limited direct links, instead proposing its own rules for management of what it regards as a domestic shipping concern.
Taiwan has banned all direct contact with China since 1949, refusing to accept the legitimacy of the communist government.

Recently, under pressure from thousands of Taiwan firms that have invested more than US$20 billion in China, Taipei has been exploring ways to ease the ban -- as long as the new links do not undermine the island's security.
A Taiwan ministry official on Tuesday described the foreign-flagging scheme as a refinement of an "offshore transshipment centre" plan unveiled in 1995.
Under the offshore transshipment centre plan, cargoes could be shuttled directly across the strait from five Taiwan ports that legally would be considered "offshore", or outside of Taiwan customs.
Cargoes originating on the mainland would not be allowed to enter Taiwan customs, while those from inside Taiwan would not be allowed to cross directly to China.
